Using EV/EBITDA as the sector card's prescribed yardstick for capital-intensive industrials, the stock trades at 76.6× (P96 vs broad peers, 225% above the sector median of 23.5×), sitting at the very top of the 50–80× band the sector card ascribes to electrical-supercycle names like Siemens and ABB — yet Schneider's contracting margins and 20%-plus PAT decline do not justify a premium over those higher-quality comparables, and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 9% over 90 days while consensus targets already imply −2.2% downside from a level near the 52-week high — grade: expensive. fundamental.thesis: Dalmia Bharat is India's fourth-largest cement producer with 49.5 MT installed capacity concentrated in eastern and southern markets, operating in a sector undergoing consolidation (UltraTech+Adani ~45% national capacity) where improving pricing discipline is gradually benefiting scale players. FY26 revenue grew +5.9% YoY to ₹14,804 Cr (a meaningful recovery from -4.8% in FY25) and PAT surged 65.5% to ₹1,157 Cr on EBITDA margin expansion to 20.8% from 17.2%, with EBITDA/tonne of ₹1,027 entering the healthy ₹900–1,100 cement benchmark; however, volume growth was only 2.2% at 60.6% utilization and realization/tonne has deteriorated sequentially (Q1FY26: ₹5,193 → Q3FY26: ₹4,800), signalling recovery is cost-driven not demand-driven. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for capital-intensive cement, at 11.55× DALBHARAT is below the Materials sector lower bound of 12× and in the P16 percentile vs broad-market peers — graded cheap — while forward P/E of 22.4× below trailing 28.4× implies earnings recovery is priced in, yet 90-day EPS estimate revisions of -18% indicate sell-side is still cutting numbers faster than re-rating targets. The biggest risk is that persistently weak volume (2.2% FY26 vs ~8–9% industry demand growth cited in the sector dossier), sub-65% utilization on a fully-built 49.5 MT base, deeply negative estimate revision momentum, and a residual PMLA/ED POC challenge of ₹93 Cr combine to make the cheap EV/EBITDA a potential value trap rather than a clean re-rating catalyst.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Zinc is India's dominant integrated zinc-lead-silver producer, commanding near-monopoly domestic zinc supply from low-cost Rajasthan mines, with silver becoming a materially growing earnings contributor alongside base metals. FY26 delivered revenue growth of +19.9% YoY to ₹40,844 cr and PAT growth of +33.6% YoY to ₹13,832 cr, with Q3FY26 accelerating sharply to +27.5% revenue and +46.2% PAT growth YoY after a soft H1FY26 (revenue -0.4%); EBITDA margins expanded to 56.8% for FY26 and PAT margins to 33.9% from ~28% a year earlier, with CFO/PAT of 1.23x confirming the earnings are real cash — not accounting artefact. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive mining business (as the sector card prescribes), the stock trades at 10.59x — P13 vs 471 market peers and a 53% discount to the broad-market median of 22.6x — firmly cheap, reinforced by a forward P/E of 13.0x below the trailing 17.5x, which prices in continued earnings growth and sits at P17 vs peers. The central risk is commodity price cyclicality compounded by the Vedanta group governance overhang, which limits the minority-shareholder premium that can be justified.

HFCL is a telecom equipment, fibre-optic cable, and defence-technology company whose revenues are heavily dependent on government/PSU tender cycles and private-telco capex, operating in a structurally growing but lumpy, order-concentrated market with thin margins and high working-capital intensity. FY26 delivered a genuine operational snapback — full-year revenue grew +21.8% YoY to ₹4,949 cr and PAT surged +75.8% YoY to ₹312 cr, with EBITDA margin expanding materially from 12.5% to 16.7% and PAT margin from 4.3% to 6.3%, recovering from a painful FY25 (revenue -9%, PAT -48.7%); however, quarterly momentum was uneven (Q2FY26 revenue dipped -4.6% YoY) and, critically, FCF landed at a deeply negative ₹-723 cr with a CFO/PAT ratio of -1.21×, meaning reported profits are not converting to cash — a serious earnings-quality flag. At a trailing P/E of 93.3× (P92 in the broad market, a 163% premium to the 35.4× market median) and EV/EBITDA of 38.5× (P80), the stock is expensive by every applicable yardstick — using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple for this capital-intensive industrials-adjacent business, even the industrials sector benchmark of 28–45× does not justify the current level when combined with negative FCF and low ROE; the forward P/E of 38.4× implies a further large earnings step-up already priced in at 93.7% of the 52-week range, leaving virtually no margin of error. The dominant risk is the extreme balance-sheet leverage (D/E 38.32) stacked on top of persistently negative free cash flow — any slowdown in government tender disbursals or a tightening of credit availability could rapidly stress interest coverage and force dilutive equity issuance.

ITI Limited is a government-owned (PSU) telecom equipment manufacturer in severe financial distress — formally declared 'sick', referred to BIFR, and reliant on a CCEA-approved state revival package of ₹41,568 cr — bearing no resemblance to the telecom-service ARPU/FCF framework in the sector card, which does not apply here. FY26 revenue collapsed 39.6% YoY to ₹2,184 cr (from ₹3,616 cr in FY25), and while the headline PAT of ₹293 cr appears to reverse FY25's loss, the core business posted an operating loss of ₹156 cr before exceptional items — the reported profit is almost entirely attributable to one-off asset-sale gains of ₹832 cr, and CFO/PAT of -0.46× confirms earnings are not cash-backed. Trailing P/E of 102.69× (vs IT/industrials sector median of 22–30×) and EV/EBITDA of 678× are economically meaningless for a core-loss-making business; P/B of 19.87× at the 96th broad-market percentile reflects a speculative government-rescue premium, not fundamental value — graded unambiguously expensive. The added danger is that auditors issued a Disclaimer of Opinion with 31 separate qualifications including internal control failures, meaning the reported numbers themselves carry significant reliability risk.

L&T Technology Services (LTTS) is a pure-play engineering R&D services company — one of India's largest ER&D players — operating across Mobility, Sustainability, and Tech segments after divesting the SWC business in FY26. FY26 full-year revenue grew 14% YoY in INR terms (₹109,959 Mn) on a continuing-operations basis, but USD revenue growth was only 8.3% and Q4 FY26 USD revenue growth decelerated sharply to just 0.3% YoY ($305.9 Mn), while PAT grew a modest 7.4% YoY to ₹12,818 Mn at an 11.7% margin — the gap between INR and USD growth is largely an INR depreciation tailwind that is now reversing given INR strengthening to 95.35. Trailing P/E of 28.2× sits at P71 vs IT sector peers and is +29% above the sector median of 21.8×; the forward P/E of 20.0× implies earnings growth is expected, but the EV/EBITDA of 18.3× is at P80 vs peers, making the stock expensive-to-fair relative to the peer set despite the 52-week low proximity (stock at only 15.1% of its 52-week range at ₹3,010–₹4,726). The biggest risk is the Mobility segment drag (−5% YoY) compounded by GenAI disruption to the ER&D services model, while the Q4 USD revenue near-stagnation signals that the FY26 large-deal TCV momentum ($855 Mn, +40% YoY) has not yet converted to sustained revenue acceleration — if macro headwinds persist into H1 FY27, consensus earnings estimates (reflected in the forward P/E) could prove too optimistic.
